# 152. ASSIGNMENT-1 TRANSFER — RECIPE SEMANTIC PARSING & STATE RECONSTRUCTION

**Origin/status:** The following constraints were discovered during the student's A1 recipe-scraping/NLP implementation and were explicitly reviewed and accepted as valid design points on 12 September 2026. They are **project observations and design requirements**. They do not establish which model family is SOTA; model selection must still be researched and benchmarked.

The module is renamed from a narrow “Recipe NER” concept to:

\[
\boxed{\textbf{Recipe Semantic Parsing \& State Reconstruction}}
\]

NER is one submodule. The full problem includes entity extraction, attributes, canonicalisation, relations, events, coreference, intermediate entities, branches/alternatives, state tracking, uncertainty and source adaptation.

## 152.1 Frozen architecture concept

```text
RECIPE SOURCE
    ↓
source-specific ingestion adapter
    ↓
immutable raw HTML / JSON-LD / API response
    ↓
recipe document normalisation
    ↓
INGREDIENT PHRASE PARSER
quantity · unit · ingredient · form · quality · observed state
    ↓
canonical ingredient/entity linker
    ↓
INSTRUCTION SEMANTIC PARSER
actions · process events · tools · time · temperature · endpoints
    ↓
coreference + intermediate-food entity tracking
    ↓
alternative / optional / conditional branch representation
    ↓
ordered state/event graph
    ↓
uncertainty / OOD detector
    ├── high confidence → accept
    ├── uncertain → stronger domain model / local SLM/LLM
    └── unresolved → human review
    ↓
STRUCTURED RECIPE STATE + PROVENANCE
```

## 152.2 Confirmed 45-point requirement register

| # | Confirmed requirement | Frozen consequence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ingredient quantity is not always numeric (`fillet`, `handful`, `chunk`, `large`, `to taste`). | Quantity schema supports numeric, range, natural-unit/count, qualitative and unknown. |
| 2 | Quantity/unit normalization can be genuinely ambiguous. | Preserve raw quantity/unit, normalized value only when defensible, type, confidence and provenance; do not invent grams. |
| 3 | Ingredient NER alone is insufficient. | Separate entities, attributes, relations, canonicalization, events, states and coreference. |
| 4 | High overall extraction accuracy can still leave many errors at corpus scale. | Report entity-level P/R/F1, exact-span metrics, per-type errors and OOD performance, not a single “accuracy”. |
| 5 | A local LLM is not assumed to beat a domain NER model. | Benchmark model families on the same gold set and splits. |
| 6 | Stronger generative models may be most useful for ambiguous/contextual cases. | Prefer confidence routing/cascades over running the largest model on every phrase. |
| 7 | If an SLM/LLM is used, plain prompting alone is not automatically sufficient. | Research constrained schemas, domain retrieval/examples and PEFT/LoRA only when benchmarked. |
| 8 | Cross-source generalization is a central failure mode. | Hold out an entire recipe source/site for OOD testing. |
| 9 | Same-site random splits can leak templates/style. | Split at source/recipe/template cluster where possible before dedup joins. |
| 10 | Ingredient phrases encode quantity, unit, ingredient, form/state, preparation and modifiers. | Preserve a multi-field phrase schema rather than only canonical names. |
| 11 | Process state and process event are distinct. | Store `observed_state`, `explicit_event` and `inferred_prior_event` separately. |
| 12 | Words such as `fillet` may denote form/cut, not proof that filleting occurred in this recipe. | Ontology separates FORM from PROCESS/EVENT. |
| 13 | One instruction can contain multiple actions/processes. | Decompose instructions into multiple ordered events. |
| 14 | Process meaning can span multiple sentences. | Track entity/state across the recipe sequence. |
| 15 | Instructions omit intermediate states/context. | State reconstruction is required; inferred states carry provenance/confidence. |
| 16 | Coreference (`it`, `them`, `mixture`, `remaining sauce`) matters. | Add coreference/entity linking across steps. |
| 17 | Recipes create intermediate entities (batter, dough, sauce, mixture, stock, paste). | State graph permits derived food entities. |
| 18 | Ingredients can merge and later split. | Representation supports many-to-one and one-to-many transformations. |
| 19 | `X or Y` is an explicit alternative, not evidence that both are present. | Preserve `OR(X,Y)`/choice groups. |
| 20 | Optional/conditional/reserved/remaining semantics change the execution graph. | Model optional branches, conditions, allocation and reserve operations. |
| 21 | Processed-state count need not be ≤ canonical recipe frequency. | Define counting unit before comparing state/event counts. |
| 22 | `f_i = Σ_s f_{i,s}` is not universally valid. | Use only when states are mutually exclusive and partition the same denominator. |
| 23 | Canonicalization is harder than singularization. | Use ontology/entity linking/synonyms with uncertainty; avoid destructive lexical collapse. |
| 24 | Ingredient concepts are hierarchical. | Keep canonical entity plus parent taxonomy (`salmon → fish → seafood`) instead of collapsing them. |
| 25 | Processes also need an ontology. | Keep specific process and parent class (`mincing → cutting`, `grilling → heating`). |
| 26 | Endpoint terms (`golden`, `soft`, `al dente`, `fragrant`) are not actions. | Represent as target/result sensory or physical states. |
| 27 | Temperature, time and physical state are transformation conditions. | Link extraction directly to `T(S_t,P_t,theta_t)`. |
| 28 | Every inferred fact needs provenance. | Record source span/layer: ingredient text, instruction, ontology inference, model inference, manual evidence. |
| 29 | Unknown/OOD entities will occur. | Use uncertainty/OOD routing rather than forced canonical mapping. |
| 30 | Rare/hard examples deserve targeted annotation. | Use active learning/hard-example mining and measure annotation efficiency. |
| 31 | Instruction understanding is semantic parsing/information extraction, not merely token NER. | Research joint or staged entity–relation–event–state models. |
| 32 | Ingredient frequency rank and contextual importance are different objects. | Keep frequency as a clean statistic; create a separate contextual-importance research task. |
| 33 | Contextual importance may use multiple independent signals. | Candidate features: frequency, cuisine specificity, graph centrality, `chi_i`, authenticity, role/quantity, process-state diversity and cross-cuisine distinctiveness. |
| 34 | Arbitrary weighted importance sums are weak science. | Study features independently; use sensitivity analysis or learn a ranker against a defined target. |
| 35 | “Important to a cuisine” is not raw frequency. | Research log-odds, TF-IDF-like specificity, PMI/MI, authenticity and Bayesian log-odds before inventing a score. |
| 36 | Cross-cuisine similarity must be explicit. | Compare distributional, graph and learned representations under defined metrics. |
| 37 | Canonical-vs-processed EDA is useful. | Analyze state diversity/entropy, cuisine-conditioned state usage and canonical vs processed rank distributions. |
| 38 | Scraping needs a real ingestion architecture. | Build source adapters, cache, retries/backoff, timeout, checkpoints, dedup and failure logs. |
| 39 | Websites differ in HTML/JSON-LD/JS/API/anti-bot behavior. | Source-specific adapters emit one canonical immutable raw schema. |
| 40 | HTTP delays/failures are ordinary operating states. | Classify transient vs permanent failures; cache/resume; do not silently drop records. |
| 41 | Web content changes over time. | Snapshot/version raw responses so NLP experiments are reproducible. |
| 42 | Model evaluation includes compute, not only F1. | Report latency, throughput, RAM/VRAM, model size and training/fine-tuning cost with quality metrics. |
| 43 | A large teacher need not be the deployed model. | Investigate distillation/pseudo-labeling only with hallucination/error auditing. |
| 44 | Recipe state reconstruction can feed the main process-state model. | Parser becomes a front-end that constructs `S_0, p_1, S_1, ...` and recovers observed `theta` fields where available. |
| 45 | Text extraction and physical plausibility are different layers. | First represent what the recipe says; later evidence/chemistry validates/enriches it. Never silently rewrite recipe text with “plausible” chemistry. |


## 152.x v8 — RECIPE GRAMMAR, CANONICALIZATION AND PROCEDURAL RECONSTRUCTION

The 45-point requirement register is extended with an explicit typed grammar.

### Core entity types

```text
INGREDIENT
COMPOUND_INGREDIENT
QUANTITY
UNIT
FORM
QUALITY
STATE
PROCESS
ACTION
TOOL
MEDIUM
TIME
TEMPERATURE
ENDPOINT
INTERMEDIATE_PRODUCT
OPTIONALITY
ALTERNATIVE
REFERENCE / COREFERENCE
```

### Core relations

```text
HAS_QUANTITY
HAS_UNIT
HAS_FORM
HAS_STATE
UNDERGOES
USES_TOOL
USES_MEDIUM
AT_TEMPERATURE
FOR_DURATION
PRODUCES
CONSUMES
PRECEDES
REFERS_TO
ALTERNATIVE_TO
OPTIONAL_IF
```

### Canonicalization is multi-level

Do not force every phrase into one label.

Keep:

```text
raw phrase
surface entity
normalized phrase
canonical ingredient
parent taxonomy
process/state modifiers
uncertainty
```

### Disambiguation

Ambiguous phrases may require:

- local sentence context,
- previous instruction context,
- recipe title/category,
- cuisine context,
- ingredient list,
- ontology constraints,
- stronger model escalation.

### Procedure synthesis from sparse recipes

If instructions are missing or incomplete, treat completion as a separate generative/reconstruction task.

Never mix:

```text
EXTRACTED_FROM_SOURCE
```

with:

```text
INFERRED_PROCEDURE
```

in the same provenance field.

### Sequential time map

A reconstructed recipe graph should support:

\[
e_t =
(
action,
inputs,
states,
tool,
medium,
\theta_t,
duration,
outputs
).
\]

Temporal constraints may be:

```text
before
after
overlaps
until-condition
parallel
optional
```

This structure will later provide supervision for process-conditioned state-transition models.

# 153. RECIPE SEMANTIC PARSING — MODEL RESEARCH LADDER

No specific model (Gemma, Llama, transformer NER, etc.) is frozen. Every rung is evaluated on identical gold/source-holdout splits and under the same ontology.

```text
RSP0  deterministic/rule + lexicon baseline
RSP1  recipe-domain token/entity model
RSP2  entity + attribute + conservative canonicalization
RSP3  relation + multi-action event extraction
RSP4  coreference + intermediate-entity tracking
RSP5  ordered state/event graph + branch/alternative semantics
RSP6  confidence/OOD routing to stronger local SLM/LLM
RSP7  active learning / PEFT / distillation if justified
RSP8  end-to-end recipe-state reconstruction feeding Project A
```

**Mandatory evaluation:** exact-span and relaxed entity P/R/F1; field-wise quantity/unit/state/process accuracy; relation/event F1; coreference/linking accuracy; state-transition consistency; alternative/optional preservation; hallucination/unsupported-field rate; calibration; held-out-site performance; latency/throughput/RAM/VRAM. A stronger model wins only when its gain survives the quality–compute frontier.

# 154. COUNTING AND RANKING SEMANTICS — FROZEN BEFORE ANALYSIS

Keep these distinct:

```text
recipe_frequency(i)  = number of recipes containing canonical ingredient i
mention_frequency(i) = number of ingredient/instruction mentions of i
state_frequency(i,s) = count under a declared unit of observed state s for i
event_frequency(i,p) = count of explicit process events p involving i
```

Never compare them without declaring the denominator. Process-state distributions may be represented as `P(s|i)` only when numerator/denominator are consistent.

Raw frequency ranking remains a descriptive statistic. Any contextual importance score is a **different research object**, must specify its target, and must not use arbitrary tie-breaking or hand-tuned weights presented as scientific truth.

# 155. MULTI-SOURCE INGESTION CONTRACT

```text
SOURCE ADAPTER
   HTML / JSON-LD / API / rendered page
          ↓
immutable source snapshot + headers + timestamp
          ↓
source parser
          ↓
canonical RAW recipe schema
          ↓
semantic parsing versions
          ↓
processed/canonical/state graph views
```

Required operational fields: source URL/ID, terms/licence status, adapter version, fetch timestamp, status code, retry class, raw hash/checksum, dedup key, parse status and failure reason. A source outage or anti-bot block is logged, not converted into missing content.

# 156. LEARNING RETURN POINT

The assignment diversion is closed as a learning source, but its confirmed research lessons stay active.

**Level-12 learning/specification is now canonicalized (§133 + PART VII §§174–183); empirical execution is the active gate.** The recipe-semantic track continues in parallel because it is a prerequisite for Level 13 recipe/cuisine representations and for Project A's real-recipe `theta`/state recovery. It does not justify skipping the Level-12 classical-vs-learned encoder gates.

# PART V — v7.0 BIO544 MIDSEM CONSENSUS → PROJECT WRITE-BACK

# 157. MIDSEM SOURCE SET, PROVENANCE RULE AND CONSENSUS POLICY

The completed midsem preparation covered the course lecture decks, instructor notes, and the core food-pairing / FlavorDB papers. This material is now reconciled into the research SSOT under one rule:

> **A course source can establish what that source reported; it does not automatically establish a universal culinary law.**

The source set used for this reconciliation includes:

```text
LECTURES / SLIDES
- Week 01 — Computational Gastronomy foundations
- Week 02 — Ahn et al. flavor network / food pairing
- Week 03 — Jain, Rakhi & Bagler Indian cuisine food pairing
- Week 02–04 — recipe data, flavor analytics, underlying chemistry
- Week 05 — world cuisine / aliasing / FlavorDB-linked analysis

COURSE NOTES
- CGAS Notes 1
- CGAS Notes 2
- CGAS Notes 3

CORE PAPERS
- Ahn et al. (2011), Flavor network and the principles of food pairing
- Jain, Rakhi & Bagler (2015), Analysis of food pairing in regional cuisines of India
- Singh & Bagler (2018), Data-driven investigations of culinary patterns in traditional recipes across the world
- Garg et al. (2018), FlavorDB: a database of flavor molecules
```

## 157.1 Evidence labels

Every course-derived statement that matters to project design should be mentally classified as one of:

```text
SOURCE FACT
    exact dataset/result/method reported by one lecture/paper

CROSS-SOURCE CONSENSUS
    same design lesson supported repeatedly across sources

PROJECT INFERENCE
    our defensible extension from source evidence

OPEN RESEARCH QUESTION
    explicitly unresolved by the source(s)

CONFLICT / DATASET DEPENDENCE
    sources disagree because dataset, mapping, controls, or sampling differ
```

Do not collapse these classes.

## 157.2 Conflict-preservation rule

When sources disagree, keep the disagreement and identify the conditioning variables instead of selecting a convenient winner.

The most important example is food pairing:

| Source | Source-specific result |
|---|---|
| Ahn et al. 2011 | North American / Western European tend positive; East Asian / Southern European tend negative/avoidance |
| Jain et al. 2015 | Indian cuisine and its regional cuisines show strong negative pairing |
| Singh & Bagler 2018 world-cuisine dataset | Indian Subcontinent appears among positive/uniform cuisines; 16 regions positive and 6 negative |
| course notes | some summaries simplify regional groupings and therefore should be treated as teaching summaries rather than a universal final taxonomy |

**Frozen inference:** food-pairing sign is **dataset-, mapping-, null-model-, and corpus-dependent**. Never encode “Cuisine X is intrinsically positive/negative” as a universal property.

## 157.3 Midsem reconciliation principle

The project uses the course to strengthen methodology, not to hard-code historical datasets:

\[
\boxed{
\text{course result}
\rightarrow
\text{methodological lesson}
\rightarrow
\text{project design constraint}
}
\]

not:

\[
\boxed{
\text{course result}
\rightarrow
\text{universal culinary truth}
}
\]

---

# 158. COURSE-LEVEL COMPUTATIONAL OBJECTS — FROZEN ONTOLOGY

The midsem material repeatedly organizes Computational Gastronomy around five data families:

```text
Recipes
Flavor profiles
Health associations
Nutrition profiles
Carbon / sustainability metadata
```

The research roadmap retains these as **separate but linkable information spaces**.

## 158.1 Recipe object

A recipe is not only a bag of ingredients. The course explicitly motivates representation of:

- ingredient identity,
- quantity,
- ingredient state/form,
- size/modifier,
- process/action,
- temporal order,
- instructions,
- possibly tools, time and temperature.

This is now fully consistent with §152–§155.

## 158.2 Flavor object

A classical ingredient flavor profile is:

\[
F_i = \{\text{empirically reported flavor molecules associated with ingredient } i\}.
\]

This is a **static evidence profile**, not the final cooked-state sensory representation.

## 158.3 Health object

Ingredient/dish ↔ disease/health associations must preserve:

- evidence source,
- association direction where available,
- study type,
- uncertainty,
- and the distinction between association and causation.

## 158.4 Nutrition object

Nutrition is represented separately from flavor chemistry:

```text
macronutrients
micronutrients
energy
serving / mass basis
provenance
```

## 158.5 Sustainability object

Carbon/environmental metadata is an optional design constraint or objective. It is not a flavor proxy and must not be silently mixed into chemical similarity.

---

# 159. FOOD-PAIRING METHODOLOGY — THE NULL-MODEL CONSENSUS

The strongest cross-source methodological lesson is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{an observed culinary pattern is meaningful only relative to an explicit null model}
}
\]

## 159.1 Classical overlap

For ingredients \(i,j\):

\[
n_{ij}=|F_i\cap F_j|.
\]

For a recipe \(R\) with \(n_R\) ingredients:

\[
N_s(R)=
\frac{2}{n_R(n_R-1)}
\sum_{i<j}n_{ij}.
\]

Cuisine-level food pairing is the average of recipe-level values under the source's declared weighting convention.

## 159.2 Real-minus-null

\[
\Delta N_s
=
N_s^{real}
-
\mathbb{E}[N_s^{null}]
\]

and standardized deviation:

\[
Z=
\frac{
N_s^{real}-\mu_{null}
}{
\sigma_{null}
}.
\]

Interpretation is strictly relative to the declared null.

## 159.3 Null ladder retained for all future cuisine-pattern claims

```text
M0    preserve recipe size; uniform ingredient choice
MF    preserve recipe size + ingredient frequency
MC    preserve recipe size + category composition
MFC   preserve recipe size + frequency + category
MX    add one further hypothesis-driven constraint only when justified
```

Possible future `MX` constraints include:

- ingredient role,
- process distribution,
- course/dish type,
- geography/season/availability,
- dietary restrictions,
- source/site,
- historical period.

## 159.4 Why this matters for the project

Changing the null answers **what explains the pattern**.

If an apparent effect disappears under a frequency-preserving null, then frequency is a plausible explanation and the project must not market the residual as an independent chemistry effect.

The project therefore requires:

```text
observed statistic
null definition
preserved quantities
effect size
uncertainty / CI
significance or Monte-Carlo probability
sensitivity to alternate nulls
```

for any claim of unusual cuisine structure.

---

# 160. FREQUENCY, CONTRIBUTION, AUTHENTICITY, FITNESS AND FOUNDER EFFECTS — NEVER CONFLATE

The midsem papers introduced several superficially similar quantities. They are now frozen as distinct concepts.

## 160.1 Frequency / prevalence

For ingredient \(i\) in cuisine \(c\):

\[
P_i^c = \frac{n_i^c}{N_c}.
\]

This asks:

> How common is ingredient \(i\) inside cuisine \(c\)?

## 160.2 Authenticity / relative prevalence

\[
A_i^c
=
P_i^c
-
\operatorname{Avg}_{c'\neq c} P_i^{c'}.
\]

Likewise define pair/triplet authenticity using the same relative-prevalence principle.

This asks:

> How cuisine-specific is the ingredient/combination?

High prevalence does not imply high authenticity.

## 160.3 Food-pairing contribution

The Jain/Ahn-style `chi_i` object is conceptually:

\[
\chi_i
=
\text{observed contribution}
-
\text{frequency-based expected contribution}.
\]

The Singh & Bagler world-cuisine paper also used an **ingredient-removal percentage-change** contribution measure.

Therefore:

> **“ingredient contribution” is not one universal formula. Always name the definition used.**

## 160.4 Fitness

Fitness belongs to a culinary-evolution model. It is a latent/model variable representing selection advantage that may reflect:

- availability,
- cost,
- flavor,
- nutrition,
- preservation,
- versatility,
- or other context.

Fitness is not directly equal to observed frequency.

## 160.5 Founder effect

An ingredient can become common because it appears early in recipes that are repeatedly copied, even without unusually high fitness.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\text{frequency}
\neq
\text{authenticity}
\neq
\text{contribution}
\neq
\text{fitness}
\neq
\text{founder effect}
}
\]

This distinction is mandatory in future ranking and cuisine-importance work.

---


## 160.x v8 — FITNESS IS A FEATURE FAMILY FIRST, A SCALAR ONLY IF THE TASK JUSTIFIES IT

The user's "fitness attribute value" idea is retained, but we do not define fitness as one arbitrary weighted sum.

Define a cuisine-conditioned ingredient fitness feature vector:

\[
\mathbf{F}_{i,c}
=
[
f_{i,c},
P_{i,c},
A_{i,c},
\chi_{i,c},
S^{pair}_{i,c},
S^{higher}_{i,c},
D^{process}_{i,c},
R^{role}_{i,c},
G^{graph}_{i,c},
H^{history}_{i,c},
X^{availability}_{i,c}
].
\]

Possible components:

### Usage
- recipe frequency,
- prevalence,
- rank,
- temporal stability if historical data exist.

### Cuisine specificity
- authenticity / relative prevalence,
- log-odds,
- TF-IDF-like specificity,
- mutual information.

### Pairing contribution
- `chi_i`,
- ingredient-removal effect,
- null-adjusted partner statistics.

### Higher-order combination evidence
- pair support,
- triplet support,
- higher-order support where data permit.

Do **not** choose arbitrary 25/35/45/55-percentile cutoffs as a default. Use:

- minimum support,
- shrinkage,
- confidence intervals,
- false-discovery control,
- held-out predictive value.

### Process-state diversity
- number/distribution of process states,
- state entropy,
- cuisine-specific process associations.

### Functional role
- staple,
- spice,
- fat,
- acid,
- binder,
- garnish,
- leavening,
- etc., where reliably inferred.

### Context / availability
Future work may include:
- geography,
- agriculture,
- trade,
- seasonality,
- economics,
- religion/dietary constraints,
- carbon footprint,
- health context.

### If a scalar is required

Only define:

\[
Fitness_{i,c}=g(\mathbf{F}_{i,c})
\]

when there is a target to learn or a transparent decision-analysis rationale.

Possible `g`:

```text
interpretable regression/ranking model
Bayesian model
multi-criteria decision analysis with sensitivity analysis
learned ranking function
```

Report ablations so the scalar does not become an unexplained "importance number".

# 161. CULINARY GRAMMAR, FINGERPRINTS AND CONTEXT — PROJECT INTERPRETATION

The world-cuisine paper offers a useful hierarchy:

```text
flavor molecules  ≈ letters
ingredients       ≈ words
recipes           ≈ sentences
cuisine patterns  ≈ grammar
```

The project adopts the **hierarchical representation idea**, not the analogy as a mathematical model.

## 161.1 Culinary fingerprint

A culinary fingerprint may include explicit, independently interpretable components:

\[
\Phi_C=
[
\text{ingredient prevalence},
\text{authenticity},
\text{pair/triplet structure},
\text{category usage},
\text{pairing/null deviations},
\text{process-state usage},
\text{recipe-size structure},
\text{graph structure}
].
\]

Do not reduce a cuisine fingerprint to one food-pairing number.

## 161.2 Context dependence

The same ingredient can have different:

- partners,
- prevalence,
- authenticity,
- contribution,
- process states,
- functional roles

across cuisines.

Therefore cuisine context is a first-class variable, not metadata to be appended after model training.

## 161.3 Higher-order structure

Pairwise analysis is a baseline.

The papers explicitly motivate analysis of:

\[
(i,j,k),\quad (i,j,k,l), \ldots
\]

but combinatorial explosion and sparse support mean higher-order statistics require:

- minimum support thresholds,
- uncertainty estimates,
- strong multiple-testing discipline,
- or learned/graph representations.

---

# 162. FLAVORDB — STATIC MOLECULAR INFRASTRUCTURE FROZEN INTO THE SSOT

FlavorDB establishes a useful separation:

\[
\boxed{
\text{ENTITY SPACE}
\leftrightarrow
\text{FLAVOR SPACE}
}
\]

## 162.1 Entity space

Contains:

- ingredient/entity,
- category,
- natural source,
- synonyms,
- food-level pairing relations.

## 162.2 Flavor space

Contains:

- flavor molecules,
- identity,
- taste/odor descriptors,
- functional groups,
- physicochemical properties,
- 2D/3D descriptors,
- ADMET-like fields,
- structural representations.

The project keeps these spaces separate and joins them with explicit identifiers.

## 162.3 Identifier discipline

FlavorDB's use of PubChem ID as a molecular primary key reinforces the SSOT rule:

```text
ingredient canonical ID  ≠ molecule canonical ID
surface name             ≠ canonical identity
CAS / synonym            ≠ unique primary key by assumption
```

Prefer stable external identifiers and preserve synonym/provenance mappings.

## 162.4 Classical molecular baseline stack

The FlavorDB paper reinforces the classical baseline ladder already frozen in Levels 10–11:

```text
molecule identity
→ descriptors
→ functional groups
→ fingerprint
→ Tanimoto / structural similarity
→ learned encoder only after baseline evaluation
```

FlavorDB used FP2/OpenBabel + Tanimoto for structural search. Our project does not freeze FP2 as the best fingerprint; it remains a historical/practical baseline example.

## 162.5 Sensory boundary

Structural similarity:

\[
T(m_a,m_b)
\]

is not the same as sensory similarity.

Ingredient food pairing:

\[
|F_i\cap F_j|
\]

is not the same as molecule structural similarity.

The project must always declare which level is being compared.

## 162.6 Evidence incompleteness

FlavorDB is not exhaustive.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\text{not recorded}
\neq
\text{chemically absent}
}
\]

Missingness, source coverage, and evidence status remain explicit model inputs/metadata.

---

# 163. RECIPE REPRESENTATION — COURSE SIMPLIFICATIONS AND OUR EXTENSION

The course deliberately begins with simplified representations because full food reality is too complex.

Two classical simplifications are:

```text
recipe     = unordered ingredient list
ingredient = unordered set of reported flavor molecules
```

These are useful baselines but ignore critical variables.

## 163.1 Missing from bag-of-ingredients representations

- quantity,
- role,
- state,
- processing,
- order,
- time,
- temperature,
- utensil/equipment,
- intermediate entities,
- alternatives/optional branches.

## 163.2 Missing from static flavor profiles

- concentration,
- sensory potency / threshold,
- interactions,
- matrix effects,
- volatility,
- reaction products,
- degradation,
- process history,
- temperature/time/pH/moisture/oxygen.

Therefore the midsem material directly supports the project's move from:

\[
\text{recipe} \to \{\text{ingredients}\}
\]

toward:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Recipe Semantic Parsing}
\rightarrow
\text{State Reconstruction}
\rightarrow
(S_0,p_1,\theta_1,S_1,\ldots)
}
\]

This is now cross-supported by the course, A1 experience, and the R1–R5 research synthesis.

---

# 164. PROCESS-CONDITIONED FLAVOR TRANSFORMATION — NOW A COURSE-ALIGNED CORE QUESTION

Multiple course sources independently identify the missing dynamic layer:

> flavor molecules can change during cooking, yet classical food-pairing analyses use static ingredient profiles.

This becomes a formal project question:

\[
\boxed{
F_i^{raw}
\xrightarrow{(p,\theta,t,\text{context})}
F_{i,t+1}
}
\]

or at full state level:

\[
\boxed{
S_{t+1}=T(S_t,p_t,\theta_t)
}
\]

## 164.1 Why the underlying-chemistry lecture matters

The course examples provide concrete evidence that processing/state changes matter:

```text
wood/lignin --pyrolysis--> guaiacol/syringol → smoky flavor/aroma
raw kidney bean --heat--> reduced phytohaemagglutinin activity/toxicity
cut onion --enzymatic cascade--> lachrymatory factor
fruit --ethylene signaling--> ripening-state changes
```

These examples are not a training dataset by themselves. They establish the mechanistic principle:

\[
\boxed{
\text{process/state}
\rightarrow
\text{chemical change}
\rightarrow
\text{sensory / health / physical consequence}
}
\]

## 164.2 Process label is not enough

The project therefore retains the stronger representation:

\[
\text{Effect}=\text{Effect}(m,p,\theta,\text{matrix/context})
\]

where \(\theta\) may include:

- temperature profile,
- duration,
- pH,
- moisture/water activity,
- oxygen,
- pressure,
- medium,
- geometry/surface area,
- ingredient interactions,
- prior process history.

## 164.3 Static FlavorDB remains baseline evidence

FlavorDB is a source for **reported ingredient–molecule associations and molecular features**.

It is not assumed to provide the cooked-state transition model.

That transition is a separate research object.

---

# 165. PERSONALIZED NUTRITION, HEALTH AND SUSTAINABILITY — BOUNDARY CONDITIONS

The course notes broaden Computational Gastronomy beyond flavor.

## 165.1 Personalized nutrition

A central lesson is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{same food}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{same physiological response for every person}
}
\]

Future recommendation systems may condition on:

- microbiome,
- blood/metabolic markers,
- anthropometrics,
- dietary history,
- user constraints.

However, the current semester research core does not need to solve personalized medicine.

## 165.2 Health associations

Health evidence must remain a separate evidence layer. Do not infer health benefit from flavor chemistry or ingredient frequency.

## 165.3 Sustainability

Carbon/environmental metadata may enter later as a multi-objective constraint:

\[
\text{sensory fit}
+
\text{nutrition/health constraints}
+
\text{sustainability constraints}.
\]

Do not mix sustainability into the flavor-similarity target unless the task explicitly requests multi-objective optimization.

---

# 166. OPEN RESEARCH QUESTIONS IMPORTED FROM THE MIDSEM PAPERS

The following questions are now explicit SSOT items because they were raised directly by the course/papers and align with our roadmap.

## Q-M1 — Robustness to data source

How robust are cuisine/flavor-pairing conclusions to:

- recipe source,
- duplicate handling,
- cuisine labels,
- aliasing,
- flavor-profile completeness,
- missing ingredients?

**Project implication:** all major empirical claims need source/site holdouts and data-ablation sensitivity.

## Q-M2 — Higher-order ingredient interactions

What changes when analysis goes beyond pairs to triplets/quadruplets?

**Project implication:** benchmark pairwise first; use higher-order statistics/graphs only with adequate support.

## Q-M3 — Ingredient quantity

How should quantities alter recipe representation, ingredient contribution, flavor state and process effects?

**Project implication:** quantity is an explicit optional field with uncertainty, not silently discarded.

## Q-M4 — Preparation and temporal order

How should recipe preparation, order and intermediate states be represented?

**Project implication:** Recipe Semantic Parsing & State Reconstruction remains a core upstream track.

## Q-M5 — Transformation during cooking

How do boiling, frying, roasting, fermentation and other processes transform flavor molecules and food state?

**Project implication:** central Project-A transition problem.

## Q-M6 — Whole-recipe taste / sensory prediction

Can we predict the sensory state of a whole recipe from ingredients, quantities, processes and conditions?

**Project implication:** long-term supervised/multitask target; do not claim solved by molecule overlap.

## Q-M7 — Novel recipe generation

How can culinary fingerprints and learned food-state representations generate recipes that are:

- plausible,
- cuisine-aware,
- palatable,
- nutritious,
- constraint-satisfying?

**Project implication:** downstream application after representation/evaluation, not first-stage novelty.

## Q-M8 — Culinary fingerprints for product design

Can explicit/learned cuisine fingerprints guide new food/beverage formulations?

**Project implication:** connect Project B search to cuisine-conditioned constraints.

## Q-M9 — Structure → odor/taste

Can chemical features predict sensory descriptors?

**Project implication:** retain classical descriptor/fingerprint baselines and learned molecular encoders; evaluate structure–sensory limits.

## Q-M10 — Artificial flavor / aroma blending

Can combinations of molecules or ingredients approximate a target flavor profile?

**Project implication:** directly supports FlavorTwin, but requires concentration/potency/context caveats.

## Q-M11 — Flavor molecules and health

Can flavor-molecule evidence be connected to health effects without conflating sensory and biomedical evidence?

**Project implication:** separate evidence graph; health claims require appropriate biomedical support.

## Q-M12 — Recipe evolution

Can copy–mutate or richer evolutionary models reproduce observed cuisine statistics and process/state patterns?

**Project implication:** useful generative/null-model baseline; matching statistics does not prove historical causation.

## Q-M13 — Contextual ingredient importance

What makes an ingredient important to a cuisine beyond raw frequency?

**Project implication:** compare prevalence, authenticity, contribution, log-odds/specificity, graph centrality, process-state diversity and learned context — never one arbitrary weighted score.

# PART VI — v8.0 POST-MIDSEM USER CONSENSUS → RESEARCH FREEZE

# 169. MULTIDISCIPLINARY CONTEXT IS A FIRST-CLASS VARIABLE

Food is not determined only by chemistry or molecular structure.

The project must preserve potentially relevant context dimensions:

```text
geography
climate
agriculture
seasonality
trade
economics
technology/equipment
culture/religion
history
health
nutrition
sustainability/carbon
availability
user/pantry constraints
```

These are not all required in the first paper.

The rule is:

> **do not claim a chemistry-only explanation when the observable pattern may be constrained by social, economic, geographic or historical factors.**

Context enters either as:

- covariates,
- controls,
- retrieval filters,
- conditioning variables,
- or explicit limitations.

# 170. HYPOTHESIS-FIRST EXPERIMENT DESIGN

Every new feature, control or learned representation must begin with a reason.

Template:

```text
HYPOTHESIS
Why should this factor matter?

MECHANISM
What causal/mechanistic story is plausible?

DATA
What variables actually measure it?

BASELINE
What is the simplest competing explanation?

CONTROL
What must be preserved/randomized?

PREDICTION
What result should occur if the hypothesis is correct?

FAILURE CONDITION
What result would weaken/reject it?

VALIDATION
What external or held-out evidence is required?
```

This applies to:

- cuisine pairing,
- fitness,
- process effects,
- recipe reconstruction,
- similarity thresholds,
- health claims,
- multimodal fusion,
- inverse design.

# 171. RESEARCH QUESTIONS ADDED IN v8

## Q-V8-1 — Cross-cuisine normalized food pairing

Which normalization / stratification scheme gives the most stable cross-cuisine comparison after controlling recipe size, ingredient vocabulary and flavor-profile coverage?

## Q-V8-2 — Fitness representation

Can a transparent cuisine-conditioned fitness vector predict ingredient persistence/usage better than raw frequency alone?

## Q-V8-3 — Higher-order support

At what support/regularization level do triplets and higher-order ingredient structures add real predictive information beyond pairs?

## Q-V8-4 — Inverse artificial-flavor reconstruction

Can a target sensory/flavor profile be approximated by a constrained mixture of molecules/ingredients with calibrated uncertainty?

## Q-V8-5 — Kitchen-constrained FlavorTwin

Given a target/missing ingredient and current pantry, can the system choose ingredient+process substitutions that preserve the target state better than static similarity?

## Q-V8-6 — Recipe reconstruction

Can a target cuisine/sensory/process fingerprint be converted into a valid sequential recipe under explicit constraints?

## Q-V8-7 — Confidence propagation

How should uncertainty from source evidence, extraction, molecular properties and process prediction be propagated into recipe-level recommendations?

## Q-V8-8 — Fingerprint / threshold selection

Which fingerprint and similarity threshold best transfer to sensory/process/cuisine tasks, and how much does the historical FP2/0.30 baseline lag modern alternatives?

## Q-V8-9 — Process prerequisite graph

Can process-context knowledge improve reconstruction of omitted recipe steps without increasing hallucination?

## Q-V8-10 — Multi-view molecular representation

Which combination of structural, physicochemical, biochemical, sensory and reactivity features is actually necessary for each downstream task?

## Q-V8-11 — Association vs mechanism

Which discovered cuisine/process associations survive stronger controls and have independent mechanistic evidence?

## Q-V8-12 — Health / drug-consumption context

Can processing-aware food-compound evidence improve retrieval of known food–drug or health interactions without making unsupported clinical recommendations?

1. **Classical baselines remain mandatory.**
2. **Encoder geometry is task/pretraining-objective dependent.**
3. **Structure, flavor, cuisine use and process state remain distinct spaces.**
4. **Ingredient representation is a set/mixture problem, not a single molecule problem.**
5. **Static molecular embeddings do not themselves “change” under cooking; composition/state changes.**
6. **Any learned model must beat strong classical baselines on leakage-controlled/OOD splits.**
7. **Compute cost, calibration and uncertainty matter alongside predictive quality.**
8. **Recipe semantic parsing/state reconstruction proceeds in parallel as the route from real text to process-state supervision.**
9. **Process-conditioned transformation remains the bridge from static FlavorDB-style knowledge to Project A and FlavorTwin V2.**
10. **Course-source conflicts are evidence about dataset sensitivity, not inconveniences to erase.**

## 168.1 Immediate next learning block

# PART VII — v9.0 LEVEL-12 CANONICALIZATION

# 174. LEVEL 12 — MASTER CONTRACT, STATUS, AND SOURCE MERGE

## 174.1 Current Level-12 status

**Learning / conceptual specification:** COMPLETE.  
**Research design:** COMPLETE enough to execute.  
**Empirical validation / code gates:** OPEN.  
**Default advanced architecture:** NONE FROZEN.  
**Level-13 entry:** BLOCKED until the empirical gates below pass.

The Level-12 program is not a request to “pick the fanciest molecular model.” Its job is to determine, under leakage-controlled and task-specific evaluation, whether learned molecular/set representations add value beyond the Level-10/11 classical baselines.

## 174.2 Non-negotiable inherited invariants

1. **Training/evaluation circularity is forbidden as the headline result.** If a model is trained to reproduce `n_ij` and evaluated only on `n_ij`, it has not demonstrated new information.
2. **E0–E3 remain mandatory.** Exact overlap, normalized overlap, fingerprint/Tanimoto aggregation and descriptor-space baselines must stand on the same split before E5–E8 claims are made.
3. **Structure, sensory similarity, process response and culinary context are distinct constructs.** A learned geometry has meaning only relative to its objective/data.
4. **Molecule encoder ≠ ingredient encoder.** `z_m` and the aggregation/interaction function that produces `z_i` are separately testable components.
5. **Static molecular identity does not itself change during cooking.** Composition, concentration, products, state, and relevance change; process modeling belongs in state-transition/reaction layers.
6. **Profile size, recipe frequency, graph degree, source count and annotation coverage are mandatory confound audits.**
7. **Attention weights are not causal chemical contribution.**
8. **Unknown is not zero; feature value is not evidence confidence.**
9. **Process-conditioned chemistry is data-limited and is the long-pole risk.**
10. **Every complexity increase requires a decision gate.**

## 174.3 Source merge provenance

This v9 Level-12 chapter merges:

- **v8 §133** — circularity rule, E0–E8 encoder ladder, classical-vs-learned gate;
- **Level-12 R&D Plan / SOT text** — evidence base, public datasets, threads T0–T9, dependency graph, phased compute plan, risk register and first-30-day actions;
- **Level-12.3–12.7 research-design Markdown** — learning objectives, molecule→ingredient aggregation, multi-view fusion, benchmark design and data-engineering contract.

The evidence status labels from the R&D plan are preserved. This merge is a structural synthesis, not a fresh literature verification pass.

## 174.4 Source bottom line and TL;DR

**Source bottom line:** Fund this program as a sequence of benchmarks, not as a pre-chosen architecture. Only four things are established well enough to freeze now: a graph neural network (GNN) can learn a useful single-molecule odor map; ECFP-style fingerprints are baselines that are very hard to beat; mixture perception can be predicted to a moderate degree from component representations; and multiresponse kinetic modeling works for well-defined Maillard model systems. Everything else in the Level 12 notes is a hypothesis that needs a decision gate before it is frozen. Process-conditioned chemistry is the least mature area and has the thinnest data.

### 174.4.1 Source TL;DR

- **What is frozen vs. open:** Graph-based odor models are proven. The Principal Odor Map (POM) was trained on "~5000 semantically labeled molecules" from GoodScents/Leffingwell (Lee et al., *Science* 2023; the public OpenPOM release has 4,983). On 400 prospective odorants its profiles were closer to the panel mean than the median panelist's were. Fingerprints stay mandatory baselines, because a 25-model/25-dataset benchmark found almost no pretrained embedding beats ECFP. Multi-view embeddings, attention fusion and pretrained-model advantages are all **hypotheses** to be tested with controlled ablations.
- **Where the real risk sits:** The two hardest layers are mixtures/ingredients and process-conditioned change. Public mixture data are small: the DREAM mixture challenge had 507 training pairs, and the best ensemble reached Pearson r ≈ 0.57. Public time-resolved process chemistry data are scarce and fragmented. So "real-time graph-node streaming" must be recast as a state-transition / reaction-network problem validated on time-resolved GC-MS or PTR-MS data.
- **What to do first:** Build the data and evaluation spine (Phase 0), then run the molecule-level representation bake-off (Phase 1), then mixtures and ingredients (Phase 2). Start process-chemistry data acquisition in parallel from day one, because it is the critical-path bottleneck. Almost all of Phases 0–2 fits on a single 24 GB consumer GPU; only foundation-model pretraining, large 3D/DFT featurization and reaction-model pretraining need multi-GPU or CPU-cluster resources.

# 175. LEVEL 12.0 — EVIDENCE FOUNDATION, STATUS LABELS, AND DATA INVENTORY

## 175.1 Status labels, corrections, and benchmark principle

**Status labels used throughout**

| Label | Meaning | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **[FROZEN]** | Established by peer-reviewed evidence or by definition | Revised only by an explicit SOT change request with new evidence |
| **[HYPOTHESIS]** | A plausible design claim with a defined test | Must pass its decision gate before it is used as a default |
| **[OPEN]** | Evidence conflicts or is absent | Needs a literature task and/or a new benchmark first |
| **[EST]** | Planning estimate by the program, not a sourced figure | Re-estimate after the first pilot run |

**Corrections preserved in the SOT [FROZEN]**

1. **SMILES is a molecular string (line-notation) representation, not a semantic or sensory representation.** It encodes connectivity (and optionally stereochemistry). Any sensory meaning has to be learned from supervision.
2. **In a molecular GNN, a node is usually an atom (and an edge a bond), not a whole molecule.** Molecule-level nodes appear only in higher-level graphs: ingredient, mixture or reaction-network graphs. The POM itself featurized each atom by valence, degree, hydrogen count, hybridization, formal charge and atomic number, and each bond by degree, aromaticity and ring membership.
3. **The message-passing update h_v^(k+1) = φ(h_v^(k), ⊕_{u∈N(v)} ψ(h_v^(k), h_u^(k), e_uv)) is a generic graph update rule, not an attention architecture.** Attention (e.g., GAT) is one specific choice of the aggregation ⊕/ψ, in which neighbor weights are learned and normalized. Sum, mean or max aggregation (GCN, GIN, MPNN, D-MPNN) are equally valid instances.

**Program-level principle [FROZEN]:** Every component is benchmarked against (a) a fingerprint + tree/linear baseline, (b) a trivial baseline (label-frequency prior, or mean pooling for sets), and (c) the published state of the art for that task, all on identical splits.

---

## 175.2 Program-level frozen knowledge (evidence base)

| # | Frozen statement | Key evidence |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | A GNN can learn a generalizable structure→odor map | Lee et al., *Science* 381:999–1006 (2023): an MPNN trained on about 5,000 GS/LF molecules; on 400 prospective odorants its profiles were closer to the trained panel mean (n=15) than the median panelist's; cross-validation AUROC 0.89 |
| F2 | The standard public single-molecule odor benchmark is GS-LF (OpenPOM) | 4,983 molecules × 138 descriptors (OpenPOM/DeepChem). Sanchez-Lengeling et al. 2019 merged GoodScents (n=3,786) and Leffingwell (n=3,561), which share 2,317 molecules, and kept descriptors with at least 30 molecules |
| F3 | Pretrained embeddings do not reliably beat ECFP | Praski et al. 2025 (25 models × 25 datasets, hierarchical Bayesian testing): "nearly all neural models show negligible or no improvement over the baseline ECFP"; only CLAMP (itself fingerprint-based) was significantly better |
| F4 | Fixed descriptors plus classical ML are strong in low-data regimes | Deng et al., *Nat. Commun.* 2023 (random forest on fixed representations performed best on most datasets) |
| F5 | Mixture perceptual similarity is predictable, but only moderately | DREAM Olfactory Mixtures Challenge: 26 teams, 507 training pairs, 46 hidden test pairs plus 50 newly collected validation pairs; the top ensemble reached median RMSE 0.08 and Pearson 0.57 |
| F6 | Human odor perception data are concentration-dependent and noisy across subjects | Keller & Vosshall 2016: 480 molecules at two concentrations, 55 subjects, 20 semantic descriptors plus intensity, pleasantness and familiarity. The DREAM 2017 challenge (Keller et al., *Science* 355:820) used 476 molecules × 49 subjects × 4,884 physicochemical features |
| F7 | Maillard chemistry can be modeled kinetically in defined systems, but the models do not transfer naively to real foods | Martins & van Boekel glucose/glycine multiresponse models: rate constants did not depend on reactant concentration, but pH changed which route dominated. A glucose/lysine kinetic model "could not explain the Maillard reaction in the chicken extract" |
| F8 | Only a small subset of food volatiles drives aroma | Dunkel et al. 2014 meta-analysis found "only about 3 to 40 genuine key odorants for each food, from a group of about 230 out of circa 10 000 food volatiles"; the de Lacy Costello et al. editorial (*Front. Nutr.* 10:1250634, 2023) says these ~230 key food odorants shape the odor profile of more than 200 foods |

| Dataset | Task | Size / labels | Access / license notes | Gaps |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **GS-LF (OpenPOM curated)** | Multi-label odor descriptors | 4,983 molecules, 138 binary descriptors | Public CSV via OpenPOM; check GoodScents/Leffingwell terms before commercial use | Binary expert labels, no concentration, long-tail labels |
| **Keller & Vosshall 2016 / DREAM 2017** | Intensity, pleasantness and 20 descriptors, per subject | 480 molecules × 2 concentrations × 55 subjects | Public (BMC Neurosci supplement; Pyrfume) | Lay panel, high inter-subject variance |

| **QuantumScents (Burns & Rogers, JCIM 63(23):7330, 2023)** | QM descriptors plus odor labels | "3.5k structurally and chemically diverse molecules" from Leffingwell (2–30 heavy atoms; C/N/O/S; the paper gives only this rounded count), 113 descriptors; 3D coordinates, PBE0 energy, dipole, Hirshfeld charges/dipoles/volume ratios | Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.8239854), CC-BY-4.0 (825.7 MB) | Single conformer; gas phase |

**Program-level data gaps [OPEN]:** (1) concentration-resolved sensory labels for food-relevant odorants; (2) quantified ingredient composition (concentration plus odor thresholds, for OAV); (3) time-resolved, compound-identified process data under controlled temperature, time, pH, a_w and O₂; (4) taste–aroma cross-modal data; (5) permissive licenses for commercial use.
